Numbers 456 through 510, 512, 617 and 618 were filed and heard on behalf of Allen 8.

generally denominated the Enemclaw Bench area) and comparing and relating them to

properties under appeal.
ECU 84. 40.030 states:
A11 property shall be assessed fifty percent of its true and fair
value in money. In determining the true and fair value of real or
personal property, the assessor shall not adopt a lower or different
standard of value because the same is to serve as a basis of taxation;
nor shall he adopt as a criterion of value the price for which the
said property would sell at auction, or at a forced sale, or in the
aggregate with all the property in the town or district; but he shall
value each article or description of property by itself, and at such
price as he believes the same to be fairly worth in mosey at the time.
such ssent is made."
The Washington State Supreme Court referring to this matter in Mason County
Overtaxed, Inc. v. Maaon County 62 Wn. 2d. 677 ( 1963) stated in its syllabus:
The provision of BCW 84. 40. 030 which directs an assessor to base
his anent of property on the ' true and fair value in money'
means that the assessment shall be basad upon market value, 1. e.,
the amount of money a purchaser, willing but not obligated to buy,
would pay an owner willing, but not obligated to sell, and the
sentimental value to, or the personal evaluation by, the owners
are no part of this valuation."

We find from the evidence the various properties had sufficient individual
characteristics to indicate they required and should have had an individual
appraisal approach made to each property. This Board, therefore, finds the 112
horizontal reduction, as applied to the values of all the properties under appeal,
was improper and not reflective of the true and fair market value of these properties.

in an effort to establish the true and fair market values of the subject properties,
finds the only indication of valuations as required by WAC 456-08- 620 produced by
the appealing property owners vas, in fact, a class contention relating to all of
the, namely, that the correct values were the values placed upon the properties
by the assessor for the year preceding the year under appeal. We find the property
owners introduced no affirmative evidence, by way of sales of comparable properties
or other indications of value of • positive nature, which this Board could use as
a basis of valuation. During the course of the hearing a continuing approach was
made upon cross-examination directed to the credibility of the assessor' s assessment
and techniques, but this again produced no affirmative evidence upon which this
Board could predicate any significant impeachment of the assessor' s testimony,
evidence or appraisal techniques. This produced no evidence upon which a value
different from the value produced by the assessor could be reasonably based.
Om the other hand, from an examination of 500 sales in the ares, the assessor
found 101 to be comparable to properties involved in these appeals. The assessor
presented direct testimony as to some of these comparable sales and related them
to specific properties involvd in these appeals. Pursuant to a stipulation of
the parties this became au evidentiary part of both the formal and the informal
appeals. The assessor stated that he personally inspected most but not all of the
comparable properties.

property owners challenged the values placed upon the improvements by the assessor
for the purpose of extracting such value from the total property value to determine
the resulting land value. The challenge were made that the assessor' s calculations
were not accurate. Despite reputed requests by the Board, both before and at the
hearing, no rebuttal evidence was introduced by the property owners to show or
establish a specific value for the extracted improvements different from the value
set by the assessor.

property appraisals has found differences in acreage values. The physical differences
found by the assessor have been reflected in the varying appraised values he has set.
It is clear the asssssor has not used an across-the-board or class appraisal approach
to the valuation of the entire Enumclaw Bench are*.

each subject property to a degree and in such manner that this Board was made
of the availability or non-availability of piped water and whether it was limited
in quantity, such as a 2 -inch main or up to and including an 8 -inch main and their
relative values. He developed characteristics with respect to road frontages and
topographical features, wen to the extent of pointing out the properties above or
below road level where road frontages were involved. Further, he developed additional
factors, such as characteristics of view, and the general water or drainage problems
of each property. He indicated such drainage problems were typical of much of the
entire Enumclaw beach area within which the appealed properties are situated.

is attributing a value to more than one road frontage adjoining a particular
tract the assessor frequently applied a different valuation to each road frontage
in recognition of its different asset value to the property being valued.

of these comparable lands to the lands under appeal.

in a fa instances introduced evidence relative to income received from their
dairy farms. The neo -detailed evidence, however, failed to establish a full true
and fair market value of the property measured by or based upon the evidence of
income. The evidence is such cases did establish, however, that the operation of

below current prices being paid for comparable lands in the area. The values

the transitional nature of the area subsequent to 1964. Mr. Sorensen testified that
historically the dairy farmer who put out cans of milk daily for pickup is gone.
It. Sorensen9 oho hes been engaged la the business of selling real estate in this

also testified that inertias in 1964 a sudden influx of people were buying smaller
acreages of. 20 to 60 acres for hams sites and were daily commuting to work in the

such values. The Board finds that the valuations made by the assessor appear to be
proper in terms of the extensive testimony which hes been presented in these appeals
and therefore affirms these values.
